doc.title: Jon-Erik Kellso interviewed by Monk Rowe, Chautauqua, New York, September 12, 1997

title: His phases of listening from Swing to bebop and fusion and back
summary: He moved from Swing to Bix, Armstrong, Condon-style jazz, Miles Davis, bebop and fusion, and has returned to small group swing.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Growing up with radio, records and family listening

blocks.x: What was happening with your personal tastes as far as the kinds of jazz you were listening to?

Good question. I’ve been through a lot of phases, I guess you could say. My first listening experiences were Swing Era, then I started sort of going backwards from there and learning about and listening to Bix Beiderbecke and Louis Armstrong, and also then getting into the Eddie Condon group with Bobby Hackett and Wild Bill Davison. And I kind of, I sort of jumped a little bit and then my dad had one Miles Davis record and I listened to that and I thought wow, this is just a completely different way to play the trumpet, but I liked that too. So then I started buying all kinds of Miles Davis records, and from that I learned about Charlie Parker, and one thing would lead to another. You’d

buy one record, looking for one particular guy, and then somebody else on that record opens your eyes and you say now I’ve got to get this guy’s records. So I went through, in high school I started to go through a period where I was buying a lot of bebop records. I liked that too. And I started to play a little bit of the groups that were kind of trying to play that style. And of course the college jazz programs generally aren’t really geared towards the older styles of music. They’re generally bebop and beyond, you know. But I was interested in that and I was very open minded and I wanted to know as much about every kind of jazz as I could really. And so I was playing in groups that were playing even like Brecker Brothers stuff in college, and you know, fusion, and I went through these different periods where I would really try to give everything a shot and learn what I could from it. And it’s funny, now, after going through all these different phases I find myself sort of back to where I started, you know, with playing mostly music from the Swing Era, give or take a little bit from traditional jazz, Dixieland, whatever you want to call it — swing music, small group swing.
